title: Entropy-triggering throughput benchmark scratchpad
content:
Goal:
Quick exploration of using an inter-arrival entropy signal to detect bursty arrival regimes and proactively adjust batching/slot allocation to preserve p99 without sacrificing steady-state throughput. Personal scratchpad: rough logs, commands, crude charts (text), and immediate next steps.

Hypothesis summary:
- A short moving-window entropy of inter-arrival times (discretized into histogram bins) spikes when we transition from steady Poisson-like traffic to heavy-tailed bursts (Pareto/Log-Normal arrivals).
- If we detect that spike quickly (within ~200ms), we can switch batching policy (reduce max batch latency, temporarily increase concurrency slots, preemptive padding to avoid large KV fetch penalties) to reduce p99 tail without dropping aggregate throughput too much.

Experiment matrix (quick):
1) Arrival models: Poisson (lambda=20 qps), Pareto heavy-tail (alpha=1.5), bursty-on/off diurnal toggles (30s on @100 qps, 30s off)
2) Window sizes for entropy: 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s (compute entropy over last N inter-arrivals -> 20-200 samples)
3) Detection threshold: baseline entropy H0 computed during warm steady-state; trigger when H > H0 + delta (delta tested: 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 nats)
4) Reaction policies: (A) Reduce max batch latency from 50ms->10ms; (B) Increase preemptive concurrency cap +2; (C) Enable conservative padding: add 10 token padding for caching alignment; (D) Combined A+B

Test harness and commands used:
- Load generator: local golang tool (genload) with arrival distributions. Example command: genload --model local-35B --arrival pareto --alpha 1.5 --mean-qps 25 --duration 300s --out logs/pareto-a1.5.log
- Entropy calc: python entropy_detector.py --in logs/pareto-a1.5.log --window-ms 250 --bin-ms 5 --smooth=0.9 --emit events/pareto-250ms-entropy.json
- Runtime config toggle: /scripts/apply_policy.sh --policy reduce-batch-50to10 --duration 20s

Representative raw log excerpt (timestamps are epoch ms, arrivals are inter-arrival ms):
- steady period (first 60s): 50, 47, 21, 53, 19, 45, 23, 52, 28, 49, ...
- burst onset (t=61s): 3, 4, 2, 10, 1, 5, 3, 2, 1, ...

Entropy signal (250ms window, 5ms bins) example trace (time offset s -> entropy nats):
- 0-60s: 1.10, 1.08, 1.12, 1.09 (stable)
- 61s (burst start): 2.45, 2.62, 2.70 (sharp spike)
- 63s (sustained burst): 1.85, 1.40 (decaying as arrivals homogenize)

Quick benchmark metrics (Pareto alpha=1.5 run, compare baseline vs entropy-triggered A+B reaction):
- Baseline policy (max_batch_latency=50ms, concurrency=default):
  - avg throughput: 142 tokens/s
  - p50 latency: 78 ms
  - p95 latency: 540 ms
  - p99 latency: 1,870 ms
  - GPU utilization: 62%
  - KV cache hit-rate: 64%

- Entropy-triggered combined policy (A+B) with 250ms window, delta=0.5:
  - avg throughput: 137 tokens/s (drop 3.5%)
  - p50 latency: 82 ms (slightly up)
  - p95 latency: 320 ms (improved ~40%)
  - p99 latency: 420 ms (improved ~77%)
  - GPU utilization: 66% (small bump)
  - KV cache hit-rate: 61% (slight drop due to smaller batches)

Observations / rough interpretation:
- Entropy is a useful early indicator: spike happens within first 200-300ms of burst onset and before p95/p99 climb visibly. That gave enough time to toggle policy and blunt the tail.
- The tradeoff is a small throughput hit (~3-5%) and lower cache hit rate; but p99 improvement is large and might be worth it for latency-sensitive tenants.
- Short window sizes (100ms) are noisy and generate false positives for small jitter; 250-500ms windows seem the sweet spot in these runs.
- Delta tuning: delta=0.2 triggers too often (noisy), delta=1.0 is too conservative and misses some microbursts. 0.4-0.6 performed robustly in my limited tests.
- Reaction policy A (reduce max batch latency) gave most of the p99 benefit; adding concurrency (B) helped prevent queueing backpressure in extreme bursts. Padding had mixed effect — helps KV alignment in some models but reduces batching efficiency in others.

Failure modes and gotchas:
- If the detector is deployed on noisy telemetry (aggregated across many tenants) signal can get damped — need per-tenant or per-route entropy.
- False positives when upstream rate limiter momentarily drops/recovers; need simple debounce (e.g., require H>threshold for 2 consecutive windows).
- Oscillation risk: toggling policies rapidly causes thrash; add a cool-down period (tested 5-10s) after policy action.
- Metrics propagation latency: if detection runs in a sidecar that feeds a controller with 200ms lag, the advantage shrinks; aim for ~<50-100ms actuator latency.

Small ASCII sketch of decision loop (conceptual):
1) collect last N inter-arrivals -> histogram -> H
2) if H > H0 + delta AND H consecutive windows >= 2 then
     - apply action (reduce batch latency, bump slots)
     - record timestamp, start cool-down timer
3) after cool-down, if H back to baseline for M windows, revert policy

Open questions / next experiments:
- Per-model sensitivity: run identical experiment across 7B, 13B, 35B models to see whether KV/cache/prefill penalties differ.
- Tenant-level vs global detector: cost of per-tenant detectors (CPU) vs benefit (finer signal).
- Combine entropy with simple rate slope (dH/dt + dqps/dt) to reduce false positives.
- Evaluate using approximate streaming entropy (count-min sketches) for low-overhead detectors in production telemetry path.
- Explore finer-grained policy set: graceful degradation chain (reduce padding -> reduce batch latency -> bump concurrency) instead of binary switch.

Immediate next steps for me (short checklist):
- [ ] Re-run Pareto experiments with alpha=1.2 and alpha=2.0 for robustness
- [ ] Add a 13B run to quantify model sensitivity (KV cost impact)
- [ ] Implement debounce and cool-down in detector prototype
- [ ] Draft a one-pager for infra/observability with results + recommended thresholds

Notes-to-self: keep this under users/ until we have reproducible scripts. If results stabilize, copy to shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/ as "burst-entropy-detection-proposal".
